metadata.title: Scientific creativity in secondary students and its relationship with STEM-related attitudes, engagement and work intentions

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a convenience sample of 780 Spanish secondary students from four high schools in the eastern region of Spain, assessed via paper-based questionnaires administered during a single class session. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights, sampling weights, or replicate-weight procedures, and it does not describe any weighting variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or a complex survey design consistent with ILSA microdata. Because the analysis is based on a non-probabilistic school-based sample rather than an international probability sample, applying ILSA-style weights would not be appropriate. For replication or extension, researchers should treat results as descriptive/inferential within the sampled schools and explicitly avoid interpreting them as nationally representative without a probability sampling frame and documented weights.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not use PISA-style cognitive achievement scores with Plausible Values; instead, it measures scientific creativity via a problem-finding questionnaire scored through fluidity, flexibility, and originality, and it measures STEM attitudes via Likert-scale items (including PISA 2015 attitude items adapted for career expectations). Because the dependent variables are not PV-based achievement outcomes, PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., complete-case exclusion or imputation), which is a reporting gap given that questionnaire-based studies typically have item nonresponse.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were recruited from four high schools in the eastern region of Spain (Valencian Community) using non-probabilistic convenience sampling. The study involved compulsory secondary education levels (first through fourth levels), with students completing paper-based questionnaires in a single 50-minute class session (including consent procedures via parents/legal tutors). The manuscript does not report additional analytic exclusions (e.g., minimum item completion thresholds) or any explicit missing-data rule; therefore, the analytic sample is treated as the full set of 780 participants who participated in the administered instruments.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 attitude items (ST113) adapted for Spanish secondary students (no PVs), compulsory secondary levels (Spain, 2021–2022)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Gender (Mann–Whitney U): males M=2.9 (SD=0.5), females M=3.1 (SD=0.4), z=4.75, p<0.001, effect size g≈0.2. Level differences (Kruskal–Wallis): p<0.001***; post hoc: level 1 vs 2 p=0.02 (g≈0.2), vs 3 p<0.001 (g≈0.4), vs 4 p<0.001 (g≈0.7).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 ST113 attitude items adapted for Spanish secondary students (no PVs) the study leveraged Gender and Secondary education level to analyze Science perceptions, finding that girls reported more positive/accurate perceptions than boys and that perceptions increased from the first to the fourth compulsory level. This indicates that strengthening gender-responsive and level-continuity science perception supports may help sustain more accurate and positive views of science across secondary schooling, though the convenience-sample design limits causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 attitude items (ST113) adapted for Spanish secondary students (no PVs), compulsory secondary levels (Spain, 2021–2022)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Gender (Mann–Whitney U): z=0.83, p=0.4 (no significant difference). Level differences (Kruskal–Wallis): p<0.05*; post hoc: level 1 vs 3 p=0.02 (g≈0.3) and vs 4 p=0.005 (g≈0.3). Descriptives: level 1 M=2.4 (SD=0.6), level 4 M=2.2 (SD=0.6).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 ST113 attitude items adapted for Spanish secondary students (no PVs) the study leveraged Secondary education level to analyze Science engagement, finding that engagement decreased from the first compulsory level to higher levels while gender differences were not statistically significant. This indicates that engagement-preserving strategies should be prioritized when students transition to later compulsory secondary years, even if gender-targeting is less critical for engagement specifically.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 attitude items (ST113) adapted for Spanish secondary students (no PVs), compulsory secondary levels (Spain, 2021–2022)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Gender (Mann–Whitney U): males M=2.5 (SD=0.8), females M=2.8 (SD=0.8), z=3.8, p<0.001, effect size g≈0.1. Level differences (Kruskal–Wallis): p<0.01**; post hoc: level 1 vs 3 p=0.03 (g≈0.4) and vs 4 p<0.001 (g≈0.5). Descriptives: level 1 M=2.9 (SD=0.7), level 4 M=2.5 (SD=0.9).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 ST113 attitude items adapted for Spanish secondary students (no PVs) the study leveraged Gender and Secondary education level to analyze Science career expectations, finding that girls reported higher expectations than boys and that expectations declined from the first to the fourth compulsory level. This indicates that career-expectation interventions should both address gender differences and counteract the drop in later secondary years, while recognizing that the convenience sample and non-causal design constrain policy inference.

main_findings.dataset_used: Scientific creativity questionnaire (Hu et al., 2010) administered to Spanish compulsory secondary students (Spain, 2021–2022)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Gender (Mann–Whitney U): males M=11.7 (SD=6.4), females M=13.4 (SD=6.4), z=4.0, p<0.001, effect size g≈0.1. Level differences (Kruskal–Wallis): p=0.097 (no significant differences); descriptives: level 1 M=11.5, level 4 M=13.2.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the Hu et al. (2010) scientific creativity questionnaire data for Spanish compulsory secondary students, the study leveraged Gender and Secondary education level to analyze Daily scientific creativity (DSCI), finding that girls outperformed boys on DSCI while DSCI did not show statistically significant differences across compulsory levels. This indicates that gender-responsive creativity support may be important, but that creativity performance may be relatively stable across levels—suggesting that interventions could focus on sustaining and broadening creativity rather than assuming a simple decline with grade.

main_findings.dataset_used: Scientific creativity questionnaire (Hu et al., 2010) administered to Spanish compulsory secondary students (Spain, 2021–2022)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Gender (Mann–Whitney U): males M=12.0 (SD=5.6), females M=14.0 (SD=5.2), z=5.5, p<0.001, effect size g≈0.2. Level differences (Kruskal–Wallis): p=0.75 (no significant differences); descriptives: level 1 M=12.8, level 4 M=12.7.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the Hu et al. (2010) scientific creativity questionnaire data for Spanish compulsory secondary students, the study leveraged Gender and Secondary education level to analyze Specific scientific creativity (SSCI), finding that girls scored significantly higher than boys while SSCI did not differ significantly across compulsory levels. This indicates that creativity development efforts may need to address gender gaps in scientific creativity, while also recognizing that grade-level differences may be minimal in this sample.

main_findings.dataset_used: Scientific creativity questionnaire (Hu et al., 2010) and STEM attitudes measures (PISA 2015 ST113 items adapted) for Spanish compulsory secondary students (Spain, 2021–2022)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Spearman correlations: DSCI–SSCI rs=0.52, p<0.001. DSCI with Engagement rs=0.05 (ns) and with Career expectations rs=0.06 (ns); DSCI with Perceptions rs=0.12, p<0.001. SSCI with Engagement rs=0.04 (ns) and with Career expectations rs=0.08* (small, p<0.05). SSCI with Perceptions rs=0.12, p<0.001. Engagement–Career expectations rs=0.5, p<0.001.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the Hu et al. (2010) scientific creativity measures together with adapted PISA 2015 ST113 attitude composites for Spanish compulsory secondary students, the study leveraged Daily and Specific scientific creativity to examine correlations with science attitudes, finding that creativity dimensions were strongly correlated with each other but only weakly related to perceptions and not significantly related to engagement, while engagement and career expectations were strongly associated. This indicates that improving scientific creativity may modestly support more accurate perceptions of science, but that boosting engagement may be more directly linked to strengthening students’ science career intentions.

data.outcome_summary: This open-access study (2021–2022 academic year) used a convenience sample of 780 Spanish compulsory secondary students from four high schools in the Valencian Community to assess scientific creativity and STEM-related attitudes. Scientific creativity was measured with the Hu et al. (2010) questionnaire, producing two total scores: daily scientific creativity (DSCI) and specific scientific creativity (SSCI), scored via fluidity, flexibility, and originality. STEM attitudes were measured with perceptions and engagement Likert composites adapted from a scientific literacy survey, and career expectations using items from PISA 2015 ST113. The study reports descriptive and non-parametric inferential results (Mann–Whitney U, Kruskal–Wallis, Spearman correlations) rather than ML prediction; no ML algorithms or PV-based achievement modeling were used. Key results include girls scoring higher on both creativity dimensions, perceptions increasing across levels, engagement and career expectations declining in later levels, and a strong engagement–career expectations correlation (rs=0.5, p<0.001). Limitations include non-probabilistic sampling, no documented missing-data handling, and a cross-sectional design that precludes causal interpretation.
